correctness.rationale: The inequality v(qs) <= q+v(s) holds for all prime q, including a q-power exponent jump of two; induction gives v(s) <= s. This proves v(n) <= n/d+d for composite n with prime support >=d. For b=2,3,4,5, the correctly normalized parity/mod-3 reversal residues yield strict inequalities excluding all sufficiently long composite reversals. Reverse primes are separately excluded by v(r)=r. All shorter prime cases were exhaustively checked by two elementary standalone routines; no infinite conclusion follows from numerical sampling.

originality.rationale: Relative to the materially inspected 2021, 2023 and 2024 primary works, the prime-free classification of the first four bases is not stated or entailed. The 2021 all-base assertion is an unproved conjecture refuted in other bases; the 2024 paper asks the actual base-classification question, and the 2023 theorem only treats decimal reversal. Prior own claims concern ordinary palindromes, not prime-power weight preservation under digit reversal. Indexed search results had no mathematical implication giving this result, although full publication priority remains unverified.
residual_risks: Absence of search hits cannot establish universal publication priority; an unindexed prior theorem or broader prime-factor-weight bound specialized to these bases could imply the classification.
The four-base classification is intentionally incomplete for bases above five; no claim is made about the least base admitting a prime.

value.rationale: This resolves the exact first four base cases of Problem 1 in the 2024 treatment of prime v-palindromes, a natural initial-segment classification. The same bases each contain known composite v-palindromes, so the exclusion is a genuinely prime-specific structural distinction. The proof handles unbounded digit lengths by elementary divisor-weight bounds and radix constraints and is not an arbitrary finite census or a routine rephrasing of a known table. No beyond-four theorem or publication priority is claimed.
